narrative:
The model estimates you have a 14% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Students who have never failed before are often those who coast on natural ability; when the final year becomes much harder, some of them suddenly struggle. Because you have no history of setbacks, the model cannot be confident you have already developed the study habits needed for this tougher stage.

The second strongest influence is the quality of your family relationships, which you described as good. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing. A supportive home environment usually helps students stay on track.

Third, your reason for choosing this school—its strong reputation—also nudges the outcome slightly toward passing. Students who picked the school for its academic standing tend to be more motivated.

To improve, focus on building consistent study routines now rather than relying on past success. Use the good family support you already have to create a structured plan for the final year, and treat the remedial courses as an opportunity to develop the resilience that students with earlier failures often gain the hard way. Taking action early can easily turn that 14% risk into a clear pass.
